newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin puts military reform on immediate agenda.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin puts military reform on immediate agenda.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin has called a meeting of his Defence Council for Thursday, adding the issue of military reform to an already long list of priorities.

Yeltsin's press secretary Sergei Yastrzhembsky told a news briefing on Tuesday that Yeltsin would chair the meeting at the General Staff headquarters. He did not disclose its agenda but said senior military commanders had been invited.
On Monday Yeltsin approved a list of seven priority tasks for the reshuffled government of Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and said they were aimed at reviving Russia's stalled economic reforms.

They included ending wage and pension delays, reforming the Soviet-era welfare system, ensuring the growth of industrial and agricultural output, fighting corruption and reducing the numbers and cost of Russia's swollen bureaucracy.

Chernomyrdin told a news conference on Monday that some of the government's practical decisions could be quite painful, but he promised to keep Russians aware of the cabinet's decisions and explain the motives behind them.
One move centres on the need to revise the 1997 budget, which both by the government and the communist-dominated State Duma lower house of parliament view as unrealistic.

Chernomyrdin and First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais are expected to brief the Duma on Wednesday on the budget for the first quarter, when most programmes were underfinanced due to poor tax revenues.
The government must then persuade the largely hostile chamber to approve its plan to cut spending by 20 percent. Deputies are due to vote on Friday.
"We hope the sequester (cuts) will be passed. Probably not immediately but there are things to work on," Chernomyrdin said on Monday, promising to work closely with the Duma.
Efforts to cut costs and fight corruption may help the government justify its budget cuts in the eyes of the public.

Thursday's Defence Council meeting will inevitably focus attention on paying for the huge but largely ineffective Soviet-era military or investing money to replace the present conscript force with a modern, professional army.
The argument about which way is more practical has led to tension between Defence Minister Igor Rodionov, a retired army general, and civilians represented by Defence Council secretary Yuri Baturin.

Yastrzhembsky said Yeltsin had ordered a halt to the reorganisation of the elite paratroop forces on Tuesday. The president's decision to restructure the force has run into stiff opposition from many officers.
Yeltsin's sacking of one-time close ally army general Konstantin Kobets from the post of deputy defence minister clearly indicated his commitment to change the military sphere.
Kobets has been accused of bribery and abuse of power. He denies the charge.
Yastrzhembsky said Yeltsin had sacked Kobets, 57, a man who backed him during a hardline coup attempt in 1991 and a revolt in 1993, after a request by military prosecutors.
Kobets, who is now in hospital, is charged with illegal dealings with commercial firms, embezzlement and illegal possession of arms.
